By the impugned Judgment and Order,

sentences.text: (a) He was convicted for commission of offence punishable u/s 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offenes (POCSO) Act, 2012 and was sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment of 10 years and to pay a fine of Rs.10,000/- and in default of payment of fine to suffer further rigorous imprisonment for three months.

entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text:
(b) He was convicted for the offence punishable u/s 366 of the Indian Penal Code and was sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment of 5 years and to pay a fine of Rs.5,000/- and in default of payment of fine to suffer further rigorous imprisonment for two months.
(c) He was convicted for the offence punishable u/s 363 of the Indian Penal Code and was sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment of 3 years and to pay a fine of Rs.3,000/- and in default of payment of fine to suffer further rigorous imprisonment for one month.
(d) He was acquitted from the charges of offence punishable u/s 344 and 506(II) of the Indian Penal Code.
(e) The Appellant was also charged u/s 376(2) of the Indian Penal Code.

But the learned Judge in his judgment at paragraph No.45 observed that though 3 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt the offence u/s 376(2) was proved, it was proved simultaneously with section 6 of POCSO and therefore he was liable for punishment u/s 6 of the POCSO Act.
2. Heard Mr. Viral Rathod, learned counsel for the Applicant, Ms. Kanchan T. Pawar, learned counsel for the Respondent No.2 and Mr. Arfan Sait, learned APP for the State.
3. The prosecution case is that the victim in this case P.W.2 was knowing the Appellant.
Her date of birth was 15/07/2002.
They were on friendly terms.
He wanted to marry her.
But she had refused.
On 30/01/2017, the Appellant took the victim to Ghatkopar Railway Station in a Rikshaw and then she was taken to Ambernath and then to Ulhasnagar.
There they stayed together.
They had sexual intercourse.
They stayed there for two months.
He performed Nikah forcibly.
In the meantime, her father had lodged complaint about her missing.
The Appellant was taking the victim to his native place in UP by train.
But the Ticket Checker questioned him and took the Appellant with him.
The victim panicked and made a phone call to her parents.
Thereafter the police swung in action.
The Appellant was arrested.
The investigation was carried out and the case was tried before the Special Judge.

4. During the trial, the prosecution examined 10 witnesses including the victim, her father, the persons at Ulhasnagar regarding their stay at Ulhasnagar, Panchas, Medical Officers, the Headmistress of the victim's school to prove her date of birth and the Investigating Officer.
The defence of the Appellant was that the victim's father was annoyed with him and therefore the Appellant was falsely implicated.
After considering the evidence, the Appellant's defence taken u/s 313 of Cr.P.C. and after hearing the arguments, learned Judge convicted and sentenced the Appellant as mentioned earlier.

sentences.text: The crucial piece of evidence in this case obviously is the evidence of the victim herself who was examined as P.W.2.
She has stated that she was residing with her parents, brothers and sisters.
She was acquainted with the Appellant as he was residing in front of their house.
He belonged to her native place.
5 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt P.W.2 and the Appellant used to have regular conversations like friends.
She used to visit his house.
The Appellant used to tell her that he would kidnap her and would take her to Ambernath and would perform marriage with her.
But the P.W.2 had not agreed with this plan.
On 30/01/2017, in the evening the Appellant called her to Mandala Police Chowky.
He asked P.W.2 to accompany him in an Autorikshaw.
They went to Ghatkopar Railway Station.
Then they went to Ambernath by train.
From there, the Appellant took her to Ulhasnagar.
He took her to a room.
It is her case that, he kept physical relations with her in that room.
They stayed together in that room for about two months.
On 02/02/2017 the Appellant had forcibly performed Nikah with her and he continued to have physical relations with her.
She had stated that those relations were kept forcibly.

She had further deposed that she was trying to return to her parents'
house, but the Appellant was not permitting her.
He used to lock her inside the house while he was going out for work.
He decided to take her to his native place at UP.
They travelled in a train.
When they reached Jhansi, she went to the restroom.
When she came out, she could not see the Appellant.
She made 6 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt enquiries with the co-passengers.
They told her that the Ticket Checker took the Appellant with him.
P.W.2 used cell phone of a co-passenger and made a phone call to her mother.
She informed about her whereabouts.
In the meantime, the Appellant returned.
The police took her to the police chowky.
The Appellant ran away.
The police officers called P.W.2's father.
P.W.2 was taken to Children's home.
On the next day her father reached there and brought her to Mumbai.
She narrated all this to her parents.
She was taken to the police station.
Her statement was recorded u/s 164 of IPC.
She gave details of the place where they had stayed together.
It is her case that, the Appellant used to give threats to her regularly.
One Arjun told her that if she informed her parents, the Appellant would be arrested.
When the Appellant came to know about the complaint filed against him, he decided to take her to his native place.

After deposing this,
she identified the Appellant in the Court.
6. In the cross-examination she admitted that she could not tell her exact date of birth and that she did not have the birth certificate.
She did not have the copy of Nikahnama.
She 7 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt did not know the name of the Maulana who had performed their Nikah.
She stated that the room where they stayed together was in a chawl.
There were 50 houses in that chawl.
There was a window to that room having sliding glass.
They used to go to public washrooms, where many people were using the same washrooms.
In this span of two months, she had gone there on many occasions and she used to meet other ladies in the vicinity.
She further admitted that her father was present when her statement was recorded.
She categorically admitted that she and the Appellant were good friends and that her parents did not like their friendship.
Her mother had even beaten her because of that and yet she continued talking with the Appellant.
Both of them were from the same native place.
She admitted that, when the Appellant established physical relations with her, she did not raise any alarm.
She never raised any alarm in the period of two months of their stay together, except on one occasion.
But she could not remember when she did that.

sentences.text: P.W.2's statement recorded u/s 164 of Cr.P.C. is produced on record at Ex.12.

In that statement,
she had not 8 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt even named the Appellant.
She had merely stated that one boy had taken her with him and had stayed together with her for about three months and that they had physical relations.
8. P.W.1 was the father of the victim.

He has stated that at the time of recording of his deposition,
the victim was about 14  years old.
He further deposed that the victim was missing from 30/01/2017.
He had initially lodged the complaint about her missing and then had lodged FIR.
The FIR is produced on record at Ex.10.
It was lodged on 07/02/2017 vide C.R.No.29/2017 at Mankhurd Police Station.
It was lodged against an unknown person u/s 363 of IPC.
According to him, on 18/04/2017, he came to know that the Appellant had kidnapped P.W.2.
Mankhurd police station had received a call from Jhansi.
He went to Jhansi and brought P.W.2 back to his house.
P.W.2 narrated the incident to him.
9. In the cross-examination he admitted that he did not like the Appellant and that P.W.2 and the Appellant used to have regular conversations.
He admitted that he had told P.W.2 not to talk with the Appellant.
The suggestion was given to him that he 9 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt himself had sent P.W.2 to the native place and had filed a false case against the Appellant.
Significantly he deposed that he handed over birth certificate of P.W.2 to the police.
Her place of birth was in Uttar Pradesh.
He had not handed over the birth certificate of P.W.2 issued at their native place.
He further added that he was having birth certificate of his daughter and he was ready to produce the same.
However, he did not produce the birth certificate.
10. P.W.3 Ritlal Pandit, P.W.4 Abdul Rehman Khan and P.W.6 Manoj Yadav - the Pancha, were examined to prove that the Appellant and the victim were staying together.
P.W.3 Pandit had given his room on rent to the Appellant.
He has stated that the Appellant stayed together with his wife for about 2  months.
One Arjun had requested this witness to permit the Appellant and his wife to stay in his room.
P.W.4 Abdul Rehman was requested by Arjun to give his room to the Appellant.
But he had not given his room to the Appellant.
P.W.6 Manoj Yadav was a Pancha.
The Appellant had pointed out the spot of incident, which was in a chawl.
The spot panchanama is produced on 10 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt record at Ex.23.
He has stated that there were sliding windows to that room.
But there was iron grill.
P.W.9 Dr. Hemant Kukade had examined the Appellant and has stated that the Appellant was capable of keeping physical relations.
P.W.7 Dr. Nishita Devendra had examined the victim on 21/04/2017.
She did not find any external injuries.
She had opined that there was no sexual assault and as per her report the exact age of the victim was not ascertained.
P.W.8 PSI Meena Varhadi had registered the complaint about missing of the victim and then had also registered C.R.No.29/2017 at Mankhurd police station.
P.W.10 P.I. Dattaram Girap was the Investigating Officer.
He had carried out the investigation including the spot panchanama etc.
More importantly, he had collected the certificate regarding the victim's birth from Municipal Corporation School.
11. The other important witness in this case is P.W.5 Saleha Ansari, who was the Headmistress of the school where the victim was studying.
She has deposed that, as per their record, the date of birth of the victim was 15/07/2002.
She had issued the certificate in that regard.

sentences.text: She had brought general register maintained by their school.
The entry in respect of the victim was at Sr.No.2583.
The entries were in Urdu.
But she produced the translated copy in English.
It was produced at Ex.19.
She also produced the translated copy of the admission form and the undertaking submitted at the time of the victim's admission.
It was produced on record at Ex.20.
In the cross-examination, she has stated that she had joined the school on 06/01/1982.
She was working as a Headmistress from 17/06/2016.
Till then, she was working as a teacher.
She admitted that till she became Headmistress, she was not authorized to issue certificate on behalf of the school.
She admitted that she did not have personal knowledge in respect of the entry in that register and that she did not have any record to show on what basis the entry was made.
She admitted that she had issued the certificate on the basis of the entries available in the register and that she had not verified the birth certificate of the victim.
She admitted that she did not have any record certifying the date of birth issued by any competent authority.
This in short was the evidence led by the prosecution.
Learned counsel for the Appellant submitted that, from the evidence on record, it is quite clear that it was a purely consensual relationship between the Appellant and the victim.
There was no force involved.
In this view, regarding crucial evidence in respect of the age of the victim; he submitted that the prosecution has failed to prove that P.W.2 was below 18 years of age at the time of incident.
He submitted that the school record shows that it was not the first school where the victim had taken admission.
The extract produced on record also shows that P.W.2 had taken admission in that particular school, of which P.W.5 was the Headmistress, from the 4 th standard.
There is no linking evidence to show how the date of birth was mentioned in the register.
In the absence of cogent evidence showing that the victim was a minor at the time of incident, no offence is made out.
Therefore the Appellant deserves to be acquitted.
He submitted that the Appellant is in custody since 11/08/2017.
Learned APP as well as learned counsel for the Respondent No.2 opposed these submissions.

Learned APP relied on section 94 of the The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act,
2015 to contend that sub-section 2 of section 94 does not require that the certificate issued should be from the first school only.

sentences.text: He submitted that even otherwise, the P.W.2 has stated that the physical relations were kept against her will.

He submitted that the Appellant has not specifically taken the defence of consensual relationship because in the statement u/s 313 of Cr.P.C. he has merely stated that since the victim's father was annoyed with him, he was falsely implicated.
14. I have considered these submissions.
The evidence of P.W.2 gives clear indication of the nature of relationship between the P.W.2 and the Appellant.
She has specifically admitted that they were on friendly terms and the Appellant had told her about his plans to take her with him and to perform marriage.
In this background on 30/01/2017, the P.W.2 met him at Mandala police chowky.
They went together to Ghatkopar Railway station.
From there they went to Ambernath by train.

sentences.text: Then the Appellant took her to Ulhasnagar from Ambernath.
Both of them went to one room.
All this shows that during all this period, P.W.2 had not resisted.
She did not raise any alarm.
This shows that after late in the evening she willingly accompanied the Appellant to a distant place and stayed with him in a room.
At no point of time, she made any grievance though she travelled in a train.
There were many people available either in the train or in the chawl, where she was taken by the Appellant.
It is not her case that at that point of time, the Appellant had threatened her or showed her any weapon and that he had forced P.W.2 to accompany him to that particular place.
After that, they stayed together for more than two months.
The evidence shows that she was going to the common restrooms etc.
There was sliding window to her room.
She could meet others.
For about two and half months she did not make any grievance.
They used to have their physical relationship.
When the Appellant came to know that a complaint was lodged against him, he decided to take her to their native place.
They travelled in a crowded train.
Even at that time, she did not make any grievance.

It appears that she was willingly 15 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt accompanying the Appellant everywhere and had not raised any grievance whatsoever though there were ample opportunities during all this period.
Even in the train the Appellant had not abandoned her, but he was taken away by the Ticket Checker and therefore the P.W.2 got panicked and called her mother.
Thereafter the Appellant was arrested.

This all clearly shows that it was a purely consensual physical relationship between the Appellant and the P.W.2.
15.
In this background, the most crucial question would be about the age of the Appellant.
The prosecution has tried to prove that she was below 18 years of age at the time of incident by claiming that her date of birth was 15/07/2002.
For that purpose, the prosecution has relied on the only evidence of P.W.5 and the documents produced by her.
The documents produced on record are at Ex.18, 19 and 20.
Ex.18 is the certificate issued by P.W.5 mentioning that according to school record the victim's date of birth was 15/07/2002.
P.W.5 has accepted that the certificate was issued based on the school record and in particular based on the general register.
The entry of the register 16 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt clearly mentions that P.W.2 was admitted in that school in the 4 th standard.
Therefore, it was not her first school.

16. Learned APP submitted that Ex.20 is the application made by the parents of the P.W.2 wherein again her date of birth was mentioned as 15/07/2002 and on this basis, the entry was made in the register.
However, that particular application was signed by P.W.2's parents.
But P.W.2's father had not identified his signature on that application.
He was P.W.1 in this case.
Her mother was not examined to identify her signature.
The entry in the register is made based only on this application.
The prosecution has not led any evidence in respect of that particular application of P.W.2's parents.
She was admitted in school on 20/06/2014.
Learned APP submitted that this application was made much before the incident and therefore there was no intention of fabricating any document.
While it is true that there was no attempt of fabricating any document, it was the duty of the prosecution to connect the link to show as to how the date of birth was mentioned in that application.
Same date of birth was mentioned in the general register based on this application 17 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt only.
This certificate at Ex.18 was issued by P.W.5 as Headmistress of the school.
Significantly P.W.1 has stated in his cross-examination that he handed over the birth certificate of the P.W.2 to the police.
That certificate is not produced by the prosecution.

He further claimed that he was having Ejahar Ali Hasan Shah vs The State Of Maharashtra on 13 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105698296/

sentences.text: birth certificate of his daughter, even then, he had not produced that certificate on record.
Therefore, adverse inference, that it was unfavourable to the prosecution, will have to be drawn.
The school record of her first school regarding her date of birth was not produced on record.

17. All these aspects considering together raise a serious doubt about genuineness of the date of birth and therefore from the evidence led in this particular case, I find that the prosecution has failed to prove the correct date of birth of the victim P.W.2.
In this view of the matter, since this was most crucial aspect, it was absolutely necessary for the prosecution to prove that P.W.2 was a minor at the time of incident.
Therefore, the benefit of doubt must be given to the present Appellant.

As discussed earlier, from the evidence it is established that it was a consensual relationship,
though the Appellant had not specifically stated so in the statement u/s 313 of Cr.PC..
He had stated that he was falsely implicated because P.W.1 was annoyed with him.
The evidence led by the prosecution itself shows that it was a consensual physical relationship.
19. Considering the evidence on record, I find that it was a consensual relationship and the prosecution has failed to prove that the P.W.2 was below 18 years of age.
Therefore this is a case where benefit of doubt has to be given to the Appellant.
In that case, the conviction recorded against the Appellant will have to be set aside.

20. Hence, the following order :
ORDER (i) The Appeal is allowed.

(ii) The Judgment and Order dated 17/10/2019 19 / 19 01-APEAL-1686-19.odt passed by Special Judge under POCSO Act, in POCSO Special Case No.479 of 2017 convicting and sentencing the Appellant is set aside.
(iii) The Appellant is in jail.
He be released forthwith if not required in any other case.
(iv) The Appeal is disposed of.
(v) With disposal of the Appeal, the Interim  Application is also disposed of.
(SARANG V. KOTWAL, J.)
